claims.text: An MLP calibrated on a limited set of ab initio snapshots can accurately capture anharmonic vibrational effects in both solid and liquid phases.
The calibrated MLP can accurately capture electron–vibration coupling in both solid and liquid phases.
Replacing explicit ab initio molecular dynamics with the transfer-learned MLP will reduce the cost of fusion-property free-energy evaluations.
The MLP workflow will retain the accuracy of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The proposed workflow pretrains an MLP on lower-cost ab initio molecular-dynamics data from simpler systems and refines it using targeted snapshots from the system under study.
Targeted training snapshots can capture the critical anharmonic and electron–vibration coupling features needed for thermodynamic calculations.
The refined MLP can be used for thermodynamic integration in both the solid and liquid phases.

Representative configurations containing anharmonic vibrational states and electron–vibration coupling features will make the MLP account for both solid lattice dynamics and disordered liquid structure.
Transfer learning enables the MLP to interpolate the free-energy landscape from a limited, carefully selected set of ab initio snapshots.
Interpolation by the MLP reduces the need for full-scale ab initio molecular dynamics while preserving subtle entropy contributions.
Rapid MLP evaluation of the free-energy landscape accelerates calculation of free-energy differences between phases.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will provide a two- to three-fold speedup over TOR-TILD for binary and moderately complex high-entropy systems.
Free-energy differences, fusion temperatures, and vibrational entropy estimates will agree with ab initio results within approximately 5–10%.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations and TOR-TILD have demonstrated high accuracy for elemental and binary systems.
TOR-TILD slows significantly for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The method is expected to apply to elemental, binary, and moderately complex high-entropy systems whose relevant configurational space is represented in the training data.
The proposed temperature domain is approximately 0.9 to 1.1 times the melting temperature.
Systems with extremely high compositional complexity or temperatures outside the stated range require further validation.
